title: Gallery Ceiling Sensors
story: An art gallery is fitting motion sensors to a square ceiling made of n × n panels. Each sensor sends beams along its row of panels, its column, and both diagonals, all the way to the walls. If a beam reaches another sensor, the two set each other off, so no two sensors may share a row, a column or a diagonal.

Some panels are glass skylights. Nothing can be mounted on glass, but beams pass straight through it. The gallery needs exactly n sensors and wants to know how many different layouts are possible before choosing one.
task: Write countLayouts(ceiling). ceiling is a list of n strings of length n; ceiling[r][c] is '.' for a normal panel and '#' for a skylight. Return the number of ways to place n sensors on normal panels so that no two share a row, a column or a diagonal.
Two layouts are different if some panel has a sensor in one and not in the other. Skylights do not block beams. If no layout exists, return 0.
constraints: Every row of ceiling has length n.

examples.explanation: There are exactly two layouts on an open 4 × 4 ceiling. Writing the sensor's column for each row, they are 1, 3, 0, 2 and its mirror image 2, 0, 3, 1. Every other try puts two sensors on a shared column or diagonal.
The skylight is at row 0, column 1. The layout 1, 3, 0, 2 needs a sensor exactly there, so it is gone. The mirror layout 2, 0, 3, 1 does not touch the skylight, so 1 layout is left.
A 1 × 1 ceiling needs one sensor, and its only panel is glass. No layout.

hints: On a 4 × 4 ceiling with 4 sensors, how many sensors can a single row hold? So how many does each row end up with?

Exactly one sensor per row. That turns the problem into a sequence of choices: pick a column for row 0, then a column for row 1, and so on. A choice is allowed only if the panel is not glass and no sensor placed so far watches it.

A sensor at (r, c) watches column c, the diagonal where every panel has row − col = r − c, and the diagonal where row + col = r + c. Keep three lists of booleans (columns, row − col, row + col) so each check is instant. Shift row − col by n − 1 so it is never negative.

Write count(row): if row == n, all sensors are placed, so return 1. Otherwise add up count(row + 1) for every allowed column, marking the column and both diagonals before the call and clearing them after. A row with no allowed panel returns 0 straight away and the search backs up.
bruteForce: Choose any n of the n² panels and check whether the sensors clash. On a 10 × 10 ceiling that is about 17 trillion ways to choose 10 panels out of 100, far too many.

Even the smarter brute force, one sensor per row and per column (every ordering of the columns), is 10! = 3,628,800 full layouts, each checked at the end. Most of them clash in the first two or three rows, so building the rest of the layout is wasted work.

a full row of skylights: no layout

walkthrough: Two observations make this manageable. First, each row holds exactly one sensor, so you only choose a column per row. Second, a panel's diagonals are identified by row − col and row + col, so "is this panel watched?" is three lookups.
Trace the open 4 × 4 ceiling, writing a layout as the chosen columns so far:

• Row 0 at column 0. Row 1 can use column 2 or 3. With 0, 2, every panel in row 2 is watched: dead end. With 0, 3, row 2 takes column 1, then every panel in row 3 is watched: dead end. So column 0 in row 0 gives 0 layouts.
• Row 0 at column 1. Row 1 can only use column 3, row 2 only column 0, row 3 only column 2. All rows filled: count 1.
• Row 0 at column 2 is the mirror image of column 1: count 1. Column 3 is the mirror of column 0: count 0.

Total 2. The most common bug is checking only one diagonal direction; on the open 4 × 4 ceiling it would also count 3, 2, 1, 0, where all four sensors sit on one diagonal. The second is forgetting to clear the three marks after the recursive call, which makes later branches see sensors that are no longer there.
solution.timeWhy: Row r has at most n − r free columns, so there are at most n! paths, and the column and diagonal checks cut most of them off within a few rows.
solution.spaceWhy: Three boolean lists of size at most 2n − 1, and a recursion depth of n.
solution.takeaway: For placement puzzles, find the structure that forces one choice per step (here, one sensor per row), and keep a small set of 'already taken' markers so each candidate is checked in O(1). Mark before recursing, unmark after.
